text.p: Setting its sights on the budding electonic commerce market, International Business Machines Corp on Monday will unveil a computer family designed to conduct a wide range of business operations on the Internet.

IBM expects the line, the latest in its AS/400 family of minicomputers, will spark new life into its hardware business, which has endured a sluggish revenue performance this year as the company works through product transitions in several of its high-end lines.
At the same time, IBM hopes to capture a lucrative slice of the market in helping companies capitalize on the changing nature of conducting electronic business or "e-business."
"We're trying to position the AS/400 as an important player in 'e-business,'" said Bill Zeitler, general manager of IBM's AS/400 division. "That's a major strategic thrust for IBM."
The new servers, dubbed AS/400e, represent a major power upgrade over their predecessors, providing up to 4.6 times the processing capabilities of earlier models.

In addition, as with earlier models, the systems are intended to run practically out-of-the-box, with operating system and other software loaded before delivery. IBM has enhanced the offering by loading non-IBM business applications as specified by the customer, Zeitler said.

The success of the model, a roughly $5 billion business, is important for IBM, which only recently saw its traditional hardware business cease to provide more than half its total annual revenues. Now, much of the company's growth is coming from its booming, albeit smaller services business.

The turnaround for AS/400 could come soon, Zeitler said, with full production of the line expected within two weeks and strong customer demand already surfacing. Some of that likely represents pent-up demand from customers who postponed orders, awaiting the new line of minicomputers.

"I think people, maybe more in the U.S. than in other places, had been waiting for this product," he said. "I expect there's a fair amount of demand out there ready for us -- in fact I'm sure there is."

Sam Albert, an industry analyst who attended a two-day demonstration of the new line hosted by IBM at its labs in Rochester, N.Y., said the revamped AS/400e also gives IBM a stage for its Domino Internet server software.

"A lot of people wondered how IBM could pay as much as they did for Lotus, but now it's clear it was a strategic move," he said. "Lotus and Domino now become visible in terms of value added and IBM is in the Internet game because of Lotus and Domino."

Aimed at small and medium-sized companies and departments in larger companies, the AS/400e can be configured for small networks or those with thousands of users. The price tag also spans a broad range, starting at about $7,995 and runs up to more than $1 million.
